procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment dated 2nd January 2023 passed by the High Court and the judgment dated 5th February 2013 passed by the trial court
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants preferred three Criminal Appeals before the High Court challenging the trial court's order. The High Court dismissed the Criminal Appeals and affirmed the order of conviction and sentence awarded by the trial Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants, being aggrieved by the High Court's judgment, approached the Supreme Court by filing the present appeals. The Supreme Court granted leave in SLP (Criminal) Nos. 837 and 1174 of 2024 and ultimately allowed the appeals, quashing and setting aside the judgments of both the High Court and the Trial Court.

directions: The judgment dated 2nd January 2023 passed by the High Court and the judgment dated 5th February 2013 passed by the trial court are quashed and set aside;

issue.issue_text: Whether the discovery of fact was distinctly within the knowledge of the maker of the statement.

facts: The prosecution relied on statements made by the accused under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, which they claimed led to the recovery of a dead body.
However, testimony from witnesses (PW-2 and PW-5) revealed that the police and the witnesses already knew about the death and the location of the body.
Specifically, the police had informed a witness about the body at around 8:00 am, whereas the accused's statements were recorded after 10:00 am.
law: Under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, for information from an accused in custody to be admissible, it must lead to the discovery of a fact.
The Court clarified that the "fact discovered" includes the object, the place it was found, and crucially, "the knowledge of the accused as to its existence."
This means the prosecution must establish that the discovered fact was "distinctly within the knowledge of the maker of the said statement."
If the fact (e.g., the location of a body) is already known to the police or others before the accused's statement, it cannot be considered a discovery based on that statement.
application: The Court applied the legal requirement of "distinct knowledge" to the case facts.
It found that the prosecution failed to prove that knowledge of the body's location was exclusive to the accused at the time they made their statements.
The evidence showed the contrary: the police and other witnesses already knew where the body was before the accused's statements were recorded.
Therefore, the information provided by the accused did not lead to the discovery of a new fact, as the fact was already known.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the condition for admissibility under Section 27 was not met. Since the police and witnesses already knew about the location of the dead body, the discovery of that fact was not "distinctly within the knowledge" of the accused when they made their statements.

issue.issue_text: Whether documents were created to rope in the accused persons.

facts.fact: The statement of a witness, Ramkumar (PW-5), was taken at Kunda police station, but he signed it at a different location, Bhatgaon.
facts.relevant_text: The evidence of Ramkumar (PW-5) would show that though his statement was taken at Kunda police station, it was signed at Bhatgaon.

facts.fact: Another witness, PW-18, admitted to signing papers without reading them and did so on the instructions of the police.
facts.relevant_text: PW-18 also admitted that he had signed the papers without reading them and that too on the instructions of the police

facts.fact: The statement of accused No. 3, recorded under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, was found to be unrelated to the discovery of the deceased's body and did not lead to any incriminating discovery.
facts.relevant_text: insofar as the statement of Dinesh Chandrakar (accused No. 3) is concerned, even the statement recorded under Section 27 of the Evidence Act is not at all related to the discovery of the dead body of the deceased. As a matter of fact, nothing in his statement recorded under Section 27 of the Evidence Act has led to discovery of any incriminating fact.

application.reasoning: The Court found the discrepancy between where a witness's statement was taken (Kunda police station) and where it was signed (Bhatgaon) to be a significant irregularity.
application.relevant_text: His evidence showed that though his statement was taken at Kunda police station, it was signed at Bhatgaon – As such, the possibility of these documents being created to rope in the accused persons cannot be ruled out

application.reasoning: This suspicion was strengthened by the admission of another witness (PW-18) who signed documents without reading them, simply because the police told him to.
application.relevant_text: PW-18 also admitted that he had signed the papers without reading them and that too on the instructions of the police

application.reasoning: The Court also noted that a key piece of documentary evidence, the statement of accused No. 3, was not actually incriminating and did not lead to the discovery of the body as the prosecution claimed.
application.relevant_text: insofar as the statement of accused No.3 is concerned, even the statement recorded u/s.27 was not at all related to the discovery of the dead body of the deceased

reasoning.conclusion: Based on the suspicious circumstances surrounding the creation and signing of witness statements, including a statement being signed in a different location from where it was taken and another witness signing papers unread on police instruction, the Supreme Court concluded that the possibility that these documents were created to falsely implicate (rope in) the accused could not be ruled out.

issue.issue_text: Whether the incriminating circumstances were proved by the prosecution.

facts: The prosecution's case against the appellants was based entirely on circumstantial evidence.
The appellants argued that the prosecution failed to prove any of the incriminating circumstances beyond a reasonable doubt.
The appellants contended that the prosecution did not establish a complete chain of circumstances that led exclusively to the conclusion of their guilt.
law: For a conviction based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances from which guilt is inferred must be fully established.
The established facts must be consistent only with the hypothesis of the accused's guilt and should not be explainable by any other hypothesis.
The circumstances must be of a conclusive nature and exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved.
There must be a complete chain of evidence that leaves no reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused.
The standard of proof is that the accused 'must be' proven guilty, not merely 'may be' proven guilty.
application: The Court analyzed the evidence presented by the prosecution against the established legal principles for circumstantial evidence.
Applying these principles, the Court found that the prosecution had "utterly failed to prove any of the incriminating circumstances against the appellants herein."
The Court determined that the chain of circumstances was incomplete and did not lead to the sole conclusion that the appellants were guilty.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution failed to prove the incriminating circumstances, as the evidence did not form a complete chain that excluded all possibilities other than the guilt of the accused.

issue.issue_text: Whether the chain of circumstances was complete.

facts: The prosecution's case was based entirely on circumstantial evidence.
The court found issues with the evidence, noting the possibility that documents were created specifically to implicate the accused.
For example, a witness's statement was signed at a different location than where it was supposedly taken.
Another witness admitted to signing papers without reading them at the instruction of the police.
The prosecution failed to prove that the discovery of the deceased's body was exclusively due to a disclosure statement made by the accused, and that no one else knew its location beforehand.
law: For a conviction based on circumstantial evidence, the law requires that several conditions must be met.
The circumstances from which guilt is inferred must be fully established.
These established facts must be consistent only with the hypothesis of the accused's guilt and should exclude every other possible hypothesis.
The chain of evidence must be so complete that it leaves no reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused.
The evidence must show that, in all human probability, the act was committed by the accused.
application: The Court applied the strict legal standards for circumstantial evidence to the facts of the case.
It found that the prosecution had "utterly failed to prove any of the incriminating circumstances" against the accused.
The weaknesses in the evidence, such as the questionable creation of documents and the failure to link the body's discovery exclusively to the accused, broke the chain of circumstances.
The evidence presented did not exclude the possibility of the accused's innocence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the chain of circumstances was not complete. The prosecution failed to establish a conclusive chain of evidence that pointed solely to the guilt of the accused and excluded all possibilities of their innocence. As a result, the Court acquitted the appellants.

cases.principle: For the lucid exposition of the expression 'fact discovered'. The principle is that the 'fact discovered' is not equivalent to the object produced, but 'embraces the place from which the object is produced and the knowledge of the accused as to this, and the information given must relate distinctly to this fact.'

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In cases based on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must fully establish circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn. The standard of proof is that the accused 'must be' proven guilty, not merely 'may be' proven guilty. The established facts must be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused and should not be explainable by any other hypothesis. The circumstances must be of a conclusive nature, excluding every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved, and must form a chain of evidence so complete as to leave no reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The prosecution has utterly failed to prove any of the incriminating circumstances against the appellants. The chain of circumstances is not so complete that it leads to no other conclusion than the guilt of the accused persons.
legal_tests_applied: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be fully established.
The facts so established should be consistent only with the guilt of the accused and should not be explainable on any other hypothesis except that the accused is guilty.
The circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency and should exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved.

There must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused and must show that in all human probabilities the act must have been done by the accused.
The accused ‘must be’ and not merely ‘may be’ proved guilty before a court can convict the accused.
policy_considerations: There is not only a grammatical but a legal distinction between “may be proved” and “must be or should be proved”, which establishes a high standard of proof as a primary principle before a court can convict an accused.
